title: Find why completion is low first
statement: Before blaming content for low completion, check when learners started, how accurate they were before stopping and how long the course is against the time they had.
example: In one grade, 69% of the learners who did little work had started only in the last six weeks of the year.
detail: Dropout analyses of a second-grade reading cohort found non-completion driven by timing rather than content: 87 of 126 minimal-work learners (69%) logged their first activity only in the last six weeks of the year, and about 13% were genuine quitters (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g2-reading/analysis/dropout-4-who.md`, line 16; `grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g2-reading/analysis/g2-completion-and-course-findings.md`, lines 84-85). There was no frustration cliff: accuracy held near 75% up to the last activity before a learner stopped, and the early accuracy of those who abandoned was within about 8 points of completers' (the same two files, lines 82-83 and 18). A headline contrast of 12.5% against about 88% completion was an artifact of course length: the short courses marked learners complete after trivial work, while the main course's denominator was 30 times larger and too long to finish in a year at the observed pace (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g2-reading/analysis/dropout-1-where.md`, lines 11 and 15).
against: One course did lose learners early, retention falling from 100% to 47% by the fourth session, but that was a session and engagement cliff, not one tied to a lesson's position (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g2-reading/analysis/dropout-1-where.md`, line 13).

evidence.quote: **The dominant non-completion driver is timing:** 69% of minimal-work students didn't start until the last ~6 weeks of the year — out of runway, not quitting. Only ~13% are genuine quitters.
87 of 126 minimal students (69%) did not log their *first activity* in any G2 reading course until the **last ~6 weeks** of the year
**No frustration cliff** in the main courses — accuracy holds ~75% right up to the last activity before a student stops; low-ability kids don't quit more than high-ability kids.
Early accuracy of abandoners (~79% pooled, first 3 days) vs completers (~87%) differs by only ~8pts — no failure cliff.
The headline contrast in the brief ("ClearFluency 12.5% vs MobyMax hole-fillers ~88%") is **an artifact of course length, not student persistence.**

The MobyMax hole-fillers are tiny (median student does ~10–11 activities, median span **1 day**, 35% one-and-done) and get marked "complete" after trivial effort. ClearFluency students do *far more work* and still show 10% complete because the denominator is 30× larger.
**Nobody finishes because the course is far too long to complete in a year at the observed pace, not because a hard lesson stops them.**
so the cliff is a *session/engagement* cliff, not a lesson-position one
